meta.title: Best Camera Under ₹60,000 in India (2026): Mirrorless Cameras That Actually Earn Their Price
meta.description: Compare the best mirrorless cameras under ₹60,000 in India by sensor, autofocus, video, lens ecosystem and warranty, with one popular resale model to skip.
meta.short_desc: Four serious mirrorless cameras for hobbyists, parents and travel photographers.
meta.tldr_pick: The Sony ZV-E10 II (16-50mm kit) is the best camera under ₹60,000 in India for most buyers in 2026: a 26 MP APS-C sensor, class-leading autofocus, 4K 60p video and a deep E-mount lens ecosystem at a body-with-kit-lens price that lands comfortably under ₹60,000.
key_takeaways: APS-C sensors are the sweet spot in this budget -- full-frame bodies in this band cost noticeably more and the lens ecosystem is smaller.
Autofocus matters more than megapixels -- Sony and Canon now lead by a generation over older Fujifilm bodies.
Lens ecosystem is a long-term decision -- Sony E-mount and Fujifilm X-mount have the broadest third-party support.
Skip legacy DSLR bargains -- the market has moved; new lenses and AF systems are mirrorless-only in 2026.
meta.who_for: Indian photographers upgrading from a smartphone, parents wanting better family photos and travel video, YouTubers starting a vlog, hobbyists who care about image quality but not full-frame cinema budgets. Not aimed at professional sports shooters or anyone buying into a used full-frame system.
meta.methodology: We compared 7 popular mirrorless cameras sold in India between ₹38,000 and ₹60,000 in mid-2026 against the four things that matter most for hobbyist use: sensor size and image quality (especially in low light), autofocus reliability for stills and video, video capabilities (4K resolution, frame rates, codec), and lens ecosystem depth (first-party and third-party). Battery life, weather sealing and weight were weighted secondarily. Pricing is the current normal sale price on Amazon India and authorised Sony / Fujifilm / Canon stores; body-only and kit-lens variants were tracked separately.

headings.text: What actually matters in a mirrorless camera under ₹60,000

faq.q: Is a mirrorless camera under ₹60,000 good enough for professional work?
faq.a: For social media, wedding secondary shooters, product photography for small businesses and stock photography, yes. For high-end commercial work or large prints, plan to step up to a full-frame body and ₹1.2-₹2.5 lakh budget.

faq.q: Do I need a kit lens or should I buy body-only?
faq.a: Buy the kit lens to start. Modern kit lenses (16-50mm, 18-45mm, 18-55mm) are optically excellent at f/5.6-f/8 and cover the most useful focal range. Add a fast prime (35mm f/1.8 or 50mm f/1.8) six months in if you want shallow depth of field.

faq.q: Sony or Fujifilm for travel photography in India?
faq.a: Sony E-mount has the broadest lens ecosystem (Sony, Sigma, Tamron, Samyang, Viltrox) so travel zooms and exotic primes are easy to find. Fujifilm X-mount's film simulation profiles suit street and portrait work straight out of camera, and the ecosystem has Sigma and Viltrox third-party lenses now.

faq.q: How much should I budget for extra batteries and a memory card?
faq.a: Budget roughly ₹3,500-₹5,000 for two spare Sony NP-FW50 / NP-FZ100 / Canon LP-E17 batteries (depending on body) and a 64-128 GB UHS-II SD card. These outlast the camera in the bag and are essential for trips.

cta.headline: Think about lenses too
cta.sub: A camera body is a 5-year purchase; the lenses you collect around it can last 15+.

body:
What actually matters in a mirrorless camera under ₹60,000

The sub-₹60,000 mirrorless market is where Indian hobbyists, parents, vloggers and travel photographers find genuinely capable cameras with modern autofocus. Five years ago, this band was dominated by entry DSLRs; in 2026, the lines have moved and mirrorless dominates. A modern entry-level mirrorless body outperforms an old mid-range DSLR on autofocus, video and live-view shooting.

What matters most is the sensor size (APS-C vs full-frame), autofocus reliability, video capability and lens ecosystem. At this price, every credible option ships an APS-C sensor -- full-frame bodies start at the ₹1.2 lakh price point. Within APS-C, Sony and Canon now lead in autofocus by a generation, while Fujifilm wins on out-of-camera colour profiles and street ergonomics.

If you only buy one thing from this list: choose the Sony ZV-E10 II with 16-50mm kit lens at its ₹48,000-₹56,000 street price. The combination of class-leading autofocus, 4K 60p video, a deep E-mount lens ecosystem, and Sony's extensive Indian service network makes it the most versatile hobbyist body in this band. The Fujifilm X-T30 II is the colour-science pick, and the Canon EOS R50 is the best ergonomics-for-stills pick.

Sensor size: APS-C is the right answer at this budget

All four options in this list use an APS-C sensor (~22x15 mm). They deliver excellent image quality up to ISO 6400, more than enough low-light performance for indoor family photos, weddings and receptions, and a usable ISO ceiling for travel video. Full-frame (35mm) bodies in 2026 still cost roughly twice as much for a body alone; at this band, APS-C is the genuine sweet spot for image quality at a sensible price.

Autofocus matters more than megapixels

Sony's Real-time Tracking AF (now in its second generation) and Canon's Dual Pixel CMOS AF II track subjects -- people, faces, eyes, animals, trains, cars -- with an accuracy that older contrast-detect Fujifilm bodies cannot match in the field. If you shoot kids, pets or fast travel scenes, the difference between modern hybrid AF and older systems is night-and-day in actual use. Megapixel counts between 20 and 26 MP are functionally similar at this level; sensor class, in-body stabilisation and the AF system matter significantly more than headline megapixel numbers.

Lens ecosystem: the multi-decade decision

The mount you pick is a 5-10 year decision. Sony E-mount has the broadest first-party and third-party support (Sigma, Tamron, Samyang, Viltrox all publish native E-mount lenses). Fujifilm X-mount has excellent first-party lenses and growing third-party support from Sigma and Viltrox, especially since 2024. Canon RF (RF-S) has strong first-party glass but third-party support is still limited. Nikon Z-mount has solid first-party lenses but is the smallest of the four.

Our top 4 picks

⭐ Top Pick

1. Sony ZV-E10 II (with 16-50mm kit lens)

Usually ₹48,000–₹56,000 (kit)
Sensor26 MP APS-C Exmor R
AFReal-time Tracking AF
Video4K 60p / FHD 120p
MountSony E-mount

The Sony ZV-E10 II is the vlogger-first body but its stills output is excellent for family and travel photography. The 26 MP APS-C sensor handles high-ISO well, and Sony's Real-time Tracking AF (now improved for v2 firmware) locks on to faces and eyes with confidence. 4K 60p video with no crop is genuinely class-leading in this band. The 16-50mm kit lens is optically solid and weight-light.

Best for vloggers, families who want both stills and video, and anyone who values Sony's broadest lens ecosystem.

✓ What works

  • Class-leading autofocus in this band
  • 4K 60p video with no crop
  • Broadest lens ecosystem (Sony + Sigma + Tamron + Viltrox)
  • Lightweight, well-built body

✗ Trade-offs

  • No built-in viewfinder (relies on rear screen)
  • No in-body image stabilisation (lens stabilisation only)
  • Plastic body, weather sealing is limited

2. Fujifilm X-T30 II (with 18-55mm kit)

Usually ₹52,000–₹60,000 (kit)
Sensor26 MP X-Trans 5 APS-C
AFPhase-detect AF
Video4K 30p / FHD 240p
MountFujifilm X-mount

The Fujifilm X-T30 II is the enthusiast-stills body in this band. Its 26 MP X-Trans sensor and Fujifilm's film simulation profiles produce out-of-camera JPEGs that suit street and portrait work without editing. The retro-styled body with manual dials feels familiar to anyone who has used a film camera. 4K 30p video is capable but trails the Sony in autofocus during recording.

Pick it for the look it produces straight out of camera and the X-mount lens ecosystem. Autofocus is decent but a generation behind Sony's.

✓ What works

  • Best in-camera colour science available
  • Film simulation modes save editing time
  • Mechanical dials suit film-camera enthusiasts
  • X-mount lens ecosystem growing

✗ Trade-offs

  • Autofocus trails Sony/Canon by a generation
  • 4K capped at 30p
  • Heavier body than Sony equivalent
Check current price →

3. Canon EOS R50 (with 18-45mm kit)

Usually ₹45,000–₹52,000 (kit)
Sensor24 MP APS-C
AFDual Pixel CMOS AF II
Video4K 30p (cropped) / FHD 120p
MountCanon RF (RF-S)

The Canon EOS R50 is the lightest body here and the best choice if you mostly shoot stills. Canon's Dual Pixel CMOS AF II is class-leading for people and pet tracking. 4K 30p is available but with a 1.6x crop; if 4K video matters more than stills ergonomics, prefer the Sony. The RF-S lens ecosystem is still small -- Canon has prioritised RF (full-frame) lens releases -- but adapted EF lenses work via the official Canon adapter.

Pick it if you want a small, ergonomic stills camera. The trade-off is the limited RF-S lens lineup and cropped 4K video.

✓ What works

  • Lightest, most ergonomic body in this band
  • Excellent people + pet autofocus
  • Wi-Fi + Bluetooth for phone transfer
  • 4K 30p available

✗ Trade-offs

  • 4K with 1.6x crop
  • Smaller RF-S lens ecosystem than Sony E-mount
  • Plastic body, weather sealing limited
Check current price →

4. Nikon Z50 II (with 16-50mm kit)

Usually ₹50,000–₹58,000 (kit)
Sensor20 MP APS-C
AFHybrid phase-detect
Video4K 60p / FHD 120p
MountNikon Z-mount

The Nikon Z50 II is the strongest Nikon entry in this band, with the new Expeed 7 processor and improved AF system inherited from Nikon's higher-end Z bodies. 4K 60p video and FHD 120p match the Sony. Nikon Z-mount lens ecosystem is solid but smaller than Sony E-mount; third-party support is improving but still behind.

Pick it if you already own Nikon F-mount lenses or have a strong reason to commit to Nikon. Otherwise the Sony is the safer long-term choice.

✓ What works

  • Modern Expeed 7 processor
  • 4K 60p / FHD 120p video
  • Nikon ergonomics for stills shooters
  • Solid Z-mount lens lineup

✗ Trade-offs

  • Third-party lens support narrower than Sony E-mount
  • Service network narrower than Canon
  • 20 MP trails Sony and Fujifilm slightly

The one we recommend skipping

⚠️ Skip

Refurbished 2018-2020 DSLR bodies at 'discounted' ₹40,000-₹55,000

TypeDSLR (not mirrorless)
AFOften phase-detect only (viewfinder)
Live ViewSlow contrast-detect
ServiceRefurb stock mostly discontinued

Marketplace listings still offer refurbished 2018-2020 DSLRs (Canon EOS 80D, Nikon D7500 etc.) at 'discounted' ₹40,000-₹55,000. These feel like bargains, but their live-view autofocus is too slow for any video work and they use older contrast-detect AF on the rear screen. Modern mirrorless autofocus is a generation ahead.

Refurbished bargains also have shorter manufacturer warranties; replacement parts (shutter assemblies, focus motors) are increasingly difficult to source. New mirrorless bodies in the ₹48,000-₹60,000 band are a strictly better choice in 2026.

The bottom line

Buy the Sony ZV-E10 II (16-50mm kit) for the most versatile hobbyist body in this band: class-leading autofocus, 4K 60p video, and the broadest lens ecosystem. The Fujifilm X-T30 II is for those who want out-of-camera colour and X-mount's growing lens lineup. The Canon EOS R50 suits pure stills shooters who value ergonomics. The Nikon Z50 II makes sense if you already own Nikon glass.

Budget an additional ₹15,000-₹25,000 in the first year for: two spare batteries (₹3,500-₹5,000), a 128 GB UHS-II SD card (₹1,800-₹2,500), a 35mm f/1.8 prime (₹14,000-₹22,000 if you want shallow depth of field), and a camera bag that fits the body + 2-3 lenses.

Frequently asked questions

Is a mirrorless camera under ₹60,000 good enough for professional work?

For social media, wedding secondary shooters, product photography for small businesses and stock photography, yes. For high-end commercial work or large prints, plan to step up to a full-frame body and ₹1.2-₹2.5 lakh budget.

Do I need a kit lens or should I buy body-only?

Buy the kit lens to start. Modern kit lenses (16-50mm, 18-45mm, 18-55mm) are optically excellent at f/5.6-f/8 and cover the most useful focal range. Add a fast prime within six months if you want shallow depth of field.

Sony or Fujifilm for travel photography in India?

Sony E-mount has the broadest lens ecosystem. Fujifilm X-mount's film simulation profiles suit street and portrait work straight out of camera.

How much should I budget for extra batteries and a memory card?

Budget roughly ₹3,500-₹5,000 for two spare batteries and a 64-128 GB UHS-II SD card.

Lens ecosystem is the multi-decade decision

Pick a mount that has first-party + third-party lens options for the next 8-10 years.
